prompt:
# Write one behaviour-tree node that ADJUSTS an existing navigator

You are writing a single node for the behaviour tree of a Unitree Go2 quadruped
navigating an indoor space it has no map of.

Below the node is an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy. The
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`. You never
touch the policy, the gait, or the joints.

**You are not writing the navigator.** A navigator already exists, it already
drives, and it will keep driving whether or not your node does anything. Your
node sits above it and revises what it asked for.

Return **one Python module**, in one fenced ```python block, and nothing else
that looks like code. Everything you want to say in prose, say outside the
fence. What the module must contain is set out in "What to return" at the end.

## How the tree runs: a layered command pipeline

Every node in the tree ticks, **every step, in order**. Nothing short-circuits
anything.

    Layer[ ports, BASE, node_1, node_2, ... ]
             ^      ^      ^
             |      |      `- each may revise the fields it declared
             |      `-------- proposes a whole command, every tick
             `--------------- publishes a few facts from the sensors

The **base** is a general indoor navigator. It gets the robot most of the way
most of the time, it handles the awkward cases, and it never declines to act.
Each later node may then adjust individual fields of what the base proposed.

This is subsumption: a competent low layer, refined by narrow higher ones. Your
node is one of the higher ones.

**So the thing you are writing is small.** It does one thing to one part of the
command, under one condition, and the rest of the time it stays out of the way.

## The one hard rule: you declare which fields you may write

Your class declares `WRITES` — the Twist fields it is allowed to touch:

```python
WRITES = ("vx",)            # may bound or set forward speed, nothing else
WRITES = ("wz",)            # may steer, but may not change speed
WRITES = ("vx", "wz")       # both. Only if the mechanism genuinely needs both.
```

This is **enforced, not advisory.** Writing a field you did not declare raises
immediately and the node is rejected. Declare the smallest set your mechanism
actually needs — a node that declares all three is claiming to be a navigator,
and it will be judged as one.

Two ways to write, and they are the only two:

```python
ports.cap(vx=0.35)       # min(|pending|, 0.35), sign kept. Never speeds up.
ports.adjust(wz=0.8)     # replaces the field outright. Last writer wins.
```

Prefer `cap` whenever the mechanism is a limit, a bound, or a "no faster than"
— it composes with other caps in any order, which `adjust` does not.

And you can see what the base asked for:

```python
pending = ports.command          # a Command(vx, vy, wz). Never None when you
                                 # tick, because the base ticks before you.
if pending.vx > my_limit:
    ports.cap(vx=my_limit)
```

**Do not call `ports.drive(...)`.** That writes the whole command and is the
base's job; it raises for a node that narrowed `WRITES`.

## Declining is a first-class outcome, and it is free

Return `Status.FAILURE` from `precondition`, or simply write nothing in `tick`,
and the base's command passes through **byte-identical**. The robot behaves
exactly as if your node were not in the tree.

That matters more than it sounds. Your node's contribution is measured by adding
it to the tree and re-running the same worlds: it can only be credited for the
episodes it changes, and it is blamed for every episode it breaks. A node that
acts only when its trigger genuinely holds is a good node. A node that fires on
every tick has replaced the base rather than supported it, and it will be
measured as having done so.

## The node contract

A leaf is one of three kinds, and the kind is the class you subclass:

- **`Condition`** — answers one question about the world and publishes it as a
  port. Never touches the Twist.
- **`Action`** — the only kind that may touch the Twist. With a narrowed
  `WRITES` it is a *modifier*, which is what you are writing.
- **`Decorator`** — wraps exactly one child and governs whether the child runs.
  Never touches the Twist itself.

Your class declares, as class attributes:

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `WRITES` | the Twist fields this node may write. See above. |
| `PORTS` | a tuple of `Port` — the typed interface between nodes. See below. |
| `PRECONDITION` | one sentence: when this node applies |
| `EFFECT` | one sentence: what this node changes |
| `TAGS` | a tuple of short strings, for retrieval |

and implements:

```python
def reset(self, scenario, rng):    # clear per-episode state. optional.
def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:   # default: always True
def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:         # Status.SUCCESS / FAILURE / RUNNING
```

**One precondition and one effect.** A node that needs two of either is two
nodes. This is not a style rule: contribution is measured by adding one node at
a time, and a node with two effects is attributable to neither.

**No coupling to a specific scenario.** Your node will be run on procedurally
generated worlds you have never seen. It may not name a room, a coordinate, a
doorway or a map. Anything it knows about the world it learns through `obs` at
tick time.

### Ports

Ports are how nodes pass information to each other. They are **not** a
blackboard: at tick time you are handed a `PortView` restricted to exactly the
ports you declared, and touching anything else raises immediately.

```python
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.IN)    # you read it:   value = ports["name"]
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.OUT)   # you write it:  ports["name"] = value
```

The port vocabulary is **closed**. These seven types and no others:

| `PortType` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `POSE` | `(x, y, yaw)` — a belief about where the robot is, never ground truth |
| `BEARING` | radians, robot frame unless the port name says otherwise |
| `SPEED` | m/s, non-negative |
| `RANGES` | an array of beam returns, metres |
| `CONFIDENCE` | `[0, 1]` — how much to trust something |
| `FLAG` | a boolean fact about the episode |
| `REGION` | an area of the floor, `(x, y, radius)` |

Three ports are always published before your node ticks, so you may declare any
of them as inputs: `goal_known` (FLAG), `pose` (POSE), `ranges` (RANGES).
Anything else you declare as an input must be published by another node earlier
in the Layer, and if nothing does, the tree refuses to build.

Publish an OUT port when the quantity you computed is genuinely useful to
someone else — a limit, a bearing, a confidence. Do not publish your own
internal state.

### What to import

Exactly these, and nothing else.

```python
import math
import numpy as np

from core.observation import Command
from nodes.contract import (Action, Condition, Decorator, Direction, Port,
                            PortType, Status)
```

Import only what you use. You will usually not need `Command` at all: a modifier
revises fields, it does not construct commands.

### What your node can see

`tick` is handed an `Observation`, frozen, one per control step:

```python
obs.t                   # sim seconds since the episode started
obs.ranges              # np.ndarray, 181 beams, metres, inf where no return
obs.range_angles        # np.ndarray, beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
obs.range_max           # 6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
obs.pose_estimate       # (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, not the truth
obs.pose_error_estimate # scalar, metres — how wrong we think the belief is
obs.contact             # bool — are we touching something right now
obs.goal                # (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of these are traps and both are deliberate:

- **`pose_estimate` is a belief.** On some scenarios a seeded random walk is
  added to it and it drifts away from the truth. Ground truth is never in
  `Observation`; the runner keeps it for scoring only.
- **`obs.goal` may be `None`**, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still
  scored against it, but this robot has not found it yet. It **latches**: once
  disclosed it stays disclosed. Your node runs on scenarios that withhold the
  goal and on scenarios that do not, so **handle `None` explicitly**. Do not
  assume a tuple.

The scan is 181 beams over a full circle, so `obs.ranges[0]` is not the front —
find the beam you want through `obs.range_angles`.

Speeds are saturated by the runner to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and
`|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Asking for more is not an error; it is just clipped.

## The task family this node has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is NOT disclosed. `obs.goal` is None until the robot has been close enough to see the goal with nothing in the way, after which it latches. Until then the task is to cover ground that has not been covered, in an indoor space with no map.

## What to base the node on

A principle card has been written for this task. **Implement this principle and
nothing else.**

```yaml
id: braking_admissible_velocity_filter
node_name: ClampTwistToBrakingAdmissible

mechanism: A commanded velocity is only permitted if the robot could still stop, under its own braking accelerations, before reaching the nearest obstacle lying on the circular arc that this velocity traces. The paper states this as a hard admissibility set, Eq. (14): a pair (v, w) is admissible iff v <= sqrt(2 * dist(v,w) * vb_dot) and w <= sqrt(2 * dist(v,w) * wb_dot), where dist(v,w) is the distance, measured ALONG THE ARC the pair traces (Section 5.2: gamma * r, with r the arc radius and gamma the swept angle to the intersection with the obstacle), to the closest obstacle on that arc. The key content is that the clearance test is arc-specific and coupled to speed, not a fixed forward stopping box: two commands with the same forward speed can have wildly different dist() because they curve into different parts of the world, and the same command is safe at one speed and inadmissible at a higher one. Why it helps: it replaces "is something close?" with "given how fast I am going and where I am actually going to sweep, can I still stop?", so the robot is free to run at full speed through open arcs while being forced — by the same single inequality — to slow down exactly as much as the geometry of its own chosen curve demands. Note the set is never empty: v = 0 satisfies the first inequality for any dist >= 0, so the filter degrades to a stop rather than to an undefined command.

trigger: Applies as a filter on every Twist about to be issued, whenever an upstream node (a frontier/coverage driver, a recovery, anything) has produced a desired (vx, vy, wz) and the current `ranges` array contains at least one finite return below `range_max`. It does NOT trigger on goal visibility, on `pose_error_estimate`, or on `contact` — it is unconditional with respect to all of those, which is the point: it is the last thing between any policy and the locomotion policy. If every beam is `inf` the filter is inert (dist saturates at range_max and no inequality binds), so it is still safe to leave permanently armed.

(5)-(9), so the arc model simply cannot predict where a vy command sweeps. MY CHOICE, not the paper's: this leaf zeroes vy (emits vy = 0) rather than passing it through, because the dist() it computes would otherwise be a prediction about a path the robot is not taking. The paper's obstacle line field built from 24 sonar beams with FIFO memory maps onto the 181 instantaneous lidar beams here; MY CHOICE: no FIFO memory is kept, only the current sweep, because the lidar gives a full circle every step and memory would inherit `pose_estimate` drift. This is why the mechanism is drift-immune: everything below is computed in the ROBOT frame from `ranges` and `range_angles`, and `pose_estimate` is never read. OBSTACLE POINTS. For each beam i with finite r_i <= range_max = 6.0 m, take p_i = (r_i*cos(a_i), r_i*sin(a_i)) in the robot frame. Inflate the body to a disc of radius rho = 0.38 m (MY NUMBER: Go2 body is about 0.70 m long by 0.31 m wide, circumscribed radius sqrt(0.35^2 + 0.155^2) ≈ 0.38 m).     dist = min(x_i) - rho, clamped to [0, 6.0]; 6.0 if the set is empty.
  - arc case: r = vx / wz, centre C = (0, r) in the robot frame. Beam i lies in
    the swept annulus iff abs(norm(p_i - C) - |r|) <= rho. For those beams let
    gamma_i in [0, 2*pi) be the angle about C from the robot's current position
    to p_i, taken in the direction of travel (sign of wz, i.e. sign-corrected so
    an obstacle behind the sweep gives gamma near 2*pi, not near 0). Then, per the
    paper, the arc distance is gamma_i * |r|; take

  - vx = 0 and |wz| >= 1e-3: pure spin sweeps no new ground for the disc model, so
    dist = 6.0 and only the wz inequality can bind (it will not, since it needs

Those are RHINO's, not a Go2's, and the true deceleration of the frozen locomotion policy is not observable through this interface. The fields mean what they say, and each one has a job:

- **mechanism** — what happens, and why it helps. This is the node body.
- **trigger** — when it applies. This is the precondition, and under the layered
  pipeline it is doing real work: outside the trigger your node must leave the
  base's command alone.
- **derivation** — how the principle becomes a rule for a Go2 with a 181-beam 2D
  scan. Where the derivation and your instincts disagree, follow the derivation:
  it is what the card is for.
- **prediction** — the falsifiable claim. **Restate it verbatim** in
  `PREDICTION`: the metric, the baseline and the minimum effect are the card's,
  not yours.
- **node_name** — what the leaf is called. Use it as the class name.

You are not told where this principle came from, and you do not need to know.
A card is a card: extracted from a paper, recalled from one, or devised from
nothing, it is implemented the same way and judged by the same harness.

If you believe a different mechanism would score better, that belief is not what
is being measured here — a node that quietly implements something else makes the
card untestable.

**If the principle genuinely cannot be expressed as an adjustment to an existing
navigator, say so in prose and write the closest honest version you can.** Some
mechanisms are whole navigators and this pipeline cannot represent them; that is
a finding about the corpus, and it is more useful than a node that pretends.

## How this node will be judged

Two steps, both automatic, neither of which you can talk round.

1. **Validity.** Your module is loaded, wired into
   `Layer[ports, BASE, your node]`, and ticked over a rollout. It has to build,
   its ports have to be satisfiable, and it must not raise. Writing a Twist
   field you did not declare fails here.
2. **Contribution.** The tree above is run over a suite of randomly generated
   indoor worlds and compared, on identical worlds, against the base alone. What
   is reported is how many worlds your node **fixed** (the base failed, the pair
   succeeded) and how many it **broke** (the reverse).

You do not write the worlds and you have never seen them. There is no
micro-world to build and no baseline to name — that is deliberate, because a
generator that writes both the mechanism and the world that judges it is
grading its own homework.

## Rules the candidate is checked against

Your module is rejected, automatically, if any of these is false. The rejection

- It parses, and it imports **only** from this list:

- Every port type is one of the seven. `EFFECT` and `PRECONDITION` are non-empty.
- `WRITES` names only `vx`, `vy` and `wz`, and the node writes nothing outside

response.text:
I couldn't write scratch files here (sandbox denied), so the module below is checked by hand rather than executed — the geometry is the part I re-derived twice, and I note the sign convention inline.

**Two places where I had to make a call, both flagged because they affect how the card gets measured:**

1. **`WRITES` has all three fields.** The derivation explicitly says the leaf emits `vy = 0`, because the arc model has no lateral term and `dist()` would otherwise describe a path the robot isn't taking. So `vy` is genuinely part of this one mechanism, not a second one — but it does mean the node declares all three, which the brief warns reads as "I am a navigator". It uses `cap(vy=0.0)` (a limit, composes) and skips the write entirely when the base already commanded `vy ≈ 0`, which I expect is nearly always.

2. **The filter declines when it doesn't bind.** The card's own trigger text says the filter is inert when no inequality binds ("dist saturates at range_max and no inequality binds… safe to leave permanently armed"). I made that literal: evaluate Eq. (14) on the *desired* pair first, and if it passes, write nothing, so the base's command passes through byte-identical. Only when the desired pair is inadmissible does the grid projection run. Without this the node would rewrite `vx`/`wz` to the nearest 0.1 grid point on every single tick — quantising the base's steering permanently, and attributing that damage to Eq. (14).

A consequence worth stating plainly: because Eq. (14)'s first inequality is `v <= sqrt(2·dist·vb_dot)`, a **negative** commanded `vx` satisfies it trivially, so a reversing recovery passes through untouched rather than being projected onto the non-negative grid and frozen at zero. That is the inequality applied verbatim; the alternative reading (project reverse onto the grid → `vx = 0`) would stall any recovery the base runs, which I judge would show up as broken episodes attributable to the projection rather than to the admissibility set.

The 189-pair grid is evaluated as one vectorised `(189, 181)` broadcast, so the per-tick cost is a couple of `arctan2` calls on ~34k elements.

```python
import math

import numpy as np

from nodes.contract import Action, Direction, Port, PortType, Status

# Candidate velocities of the card: vx in {0.0..0.8} x wz in {-1.0..1.0}, step 0.1.
# Built once at import; the pair (0.0, 0.0) is always present, so the admissible
# set is never empty and a command always exists.
_GVX, _GWZ = (a.ravel() for a in np.meshgrid(
    np.round(np.arange(0.0, 0.801, 0.1), 3),
    np.round(np.arange(-1.0, 1.001, 0.1), 3),
    indexing="ij"))


class ClampTwistToBrakingAdmissible(Action):
    """Braking-admissible velocity filter, Eq. (14) of the dynamic-window paper.

    A commanded pair (vx, wz) is permitted only if the robot could still brake to
    a stop, under its own braking accelerations, before reaching the nearest
    obstacle lying on the circular arc that this very pair traces:

        vx <= sqrt(2 * dist(vx, wz) * VB_DOT)   and
       |wz| <= sqrt(2 * dist(vx, wz) * WB_DOT)

    where dist is measured ALONG THAT ARC (Section 5.2: gamma * r), not through a
    fixed forward stopping box. That coupling is the whole content: two commands
    with the same forward speed sweep different parts of the room and so get
    different dist, and one command is admissible slowly and inadmissible quickly.

    Revises vx and wz, because those are the two terms of the inequality, and caps
    vy to zero, because the paper's arc model carries no lateral term (Section 3.1,
    "the translational velocity always leads in the steering direction") and any
    dist computed while the body is also sliding sideways is a prediction about a
    path the robot is not on.

    Declines -- writing nothing, so the base's command passes through unchanged --
    when no beam returns inside range_max (dist saturates, nothing binds), and
    when the base's own command already satisfies both inequalities. Reverse
    commands satisfy the first inequality trivially for any dist >= 0, so a
    reversing recovery is passed through rather than projected onto the
    non-negative candidate grid.

    Everything below is computed in the ROBOT frame from ranges/range_angles.
    pose_estimate is never read, so the mechanism is immune to pose drift, and no
    FIFO obstacle memory is kept: the lidar gives a full circle every step, and
    remembered points would inherit exactly the drift this avoids.
    """

    WRITES = ("vx", "vy", "wz")
    PORTS = (Port("braking_speed_limit", PortType.SPEED, Direction.OUT),)
    PRECONDITION = (
        "A twist has been proposed upstream and the current scan holds at least "
        "one finite return inside range_max."
    )
    EFFECT = (
        "Replaces the proposed forward and yaw rates with the nearest pair that "
        "could still brake to a stop before the closest obstacle on the arc that "
        "pair traces."
    )
    TAGS = ("safety", "velocity-filter", "braking-distance", "arc-clearance",
            "collision-avoidance", "reactive", "drift-immune")

    # Go2 body is about 0.70 m by 0.31 m; circumscribed disc radius.
    RHO = 0.38
    # Braking accelerations: not RHINO's. Chosen so the full command range is
    # nulled in about a second of tracking (0.8 m/s -> 0 in 1.0 s, 1.0 rad/s -> 0
    # in 0.67 s). VB_DOT is the single safety knob.
    VB_DOT = 0.8
    WB_DOT = 1.5
    VX_MAX = 0.8
    WZ_MAX = 1.0
    # Below this yaw rate the arc radius blows up and the sweep is a straight line.
    STRAIGHT_EPS = 1e-3
    TOL = 1e-9

    def reset(self, scenario, rng):
        """No per-episode state: every tick is decided from that tick's scan alone."""

    def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:
        ranges = np.asarray(obs.ranges, dtype=float)
        return bool(np.any(np.isfinite(ranges) & (ranges <= float(obs.range_max))))

    def _clearance(self, px, py, v, w, r_max):
        """Arc distance to the nearest obstacle for each candidate pair.

        px, py are obstacle points in the robot frame; v, w are equal-length
        candidate arrays. Returns dist(v, w) per Section 5.2, clamped to
        [0, r_max], already reduced by the body inflation RHO.
        """
        dist = np.full(v.shape, r_max, dtype=float)
        if px.size == 0:
            return dist

        straight = np.abs(w) < self.STRAIGHT_EPS
        if np.any(straight):
            band = (np.abs(py) <= self.RHO) & (px > 0.0)
            ahead = float(np.min(px[band])) - self.RHO if np.any(band) else r_max
            dist[straight] = min(max(ahead, 0.0), r_max)

        # vx == 0 with real yaw rate: a spin sweeps no new ground for a disc, so
        # dist saturates and only the wz inequality could bind (it cannot).
        turning = ~straight
        dist[turning & (v <= 0.0)] = r_max

        arc = turning & (v > 0.0)
        if not np.any(arc):
            return dist

        r = v[arc] / w[arc]                      # signed arc radius, centre at (0, r)
        absr = np.abs(r)
        rc = r[:, None]
        dy = py[None, :] - rc
        on_arc = np.abs(np.hypot(px[None, :], dy) - absr[:, None]) <= self.RHO

        # Angle about the centre from the robot (origin) to each obstacle point.
        # From the centre, the robot is at (0, -r) and the point at (px, py - r);
        # cross = r*px and dot = r*r - r*py give the signed swept angle.
        delta = np.arctan2(rc * px[None, :], rc * rc - rc * py[None, :])
        # Sign-correct by the direction of travel, then wrap: a point behind the
        # sweep lands near 2*pi rather than near 0.
        gamma = np.mod(delta * np.sign(w[arc])[:, None], 2.0 * math.pi)

        along = np.where(on_arc, gamma * absr[:, None], np.inf)
        dist[arc] = np.clip(np.min(along, axis=1) - self.RHO, 0.0, r_max)
        return dist

    def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:
        pending = ports.command

        ranges = np.asarray(obs.ranges, dtype=float)
        angles = np.asarray(obs.range_angles, dtype=float)
        r_max = float(obs.range_max)
        hit = np.isfinite(ranges) & (ranges <= r_max)
        if not np.any(hit):
            # Nothing in sight: dist saturates everywhere and no inequality binds.
            return Status.FAILURE

        rr = ranges[hit]
        aa = angles[hit]
        px = rr * np.cos(aa)
        py = rr * np.sin(aa)

        vx_d = float(np.clip(pending.vx, -self.VX_MAX, self.VX_MAX))
        wz_d = float(np.clip(pending.wz, -self.WZ_MAX, self.WZ_MAX))

        # The arc model only describes motion with no lateral term, so the sideways
        # component goes before any clearance computed from it can be trusted.
        if abs(pending.vy) > 1e-6:
            ports.cap(vy=0.0)

        # Clearance on the arc the base actually asked for. A reverse command is
        # evaluated on the vx = 0 sweep: its own inequality is satisfied by any
        # negative speed, so this only ever decides the wz term for it.
        d_des = float(self._clearance(
            px, py,
            np.array([max(vx_d, 0.0)]), np.array([wz_d]),
            r_max)[0])

        v_ceiling = math.sqrt(2.0 * d_des * self.VB_DOT)
        ports["braking_speed_limit"] = float(v_ceiling)

        if (vx_d <= v_ceiling + self.TOL
                and abs(wz_d) <= math.sqrt(2.0 * d_des * self.WB_DOT) + self.TOL):
            # Already admissible: leave the base's steering and speed untouched.
            return Status.SUCCESS

        dist = self._clearance(px, py, _GVX, _GWZ, r_max)
        admissible = ((_GVX <= np.sqrt(2.0 * dist * self.VB_DOT) + self.TOL)
                      & (np.abs(_GWZ) <= np.sqrt(2.0 * dist * self.WB_DOT) + self.TOL))

        if not np.any(admissible):
            # Unreachable -- (0, 0) always satisfies both -- but the filter must
            # degrade to a stop, never to an undefined command.
            ports.adjust(vx=0.0, wz=0.0)
            return Status.SUCCESS

        # Nearest-point projection onto the admissible set, with a rad/s of turn
        # error costing half what a m/s of speed error costs, so the leaf perturbs
        # the upstream command only as far as Eq. (14) demands.
        cost = (_GVX - vx_d) ** 2 + (0.5 * (_GWZ - wz_d)) ** 2
        best = int(np.argmin(np.where(admissible, cost, np.inf)))
        ports.adjust(vx=float(_GVX[best]), wz=float(_GWZ[best]))
        return Status.SUCCESS


PREDICTION = {
    "metric": "collisions",
    "baseline": "reactive_avoid",
    "min_effect": 0.5,
    "cost_metric": "time_to_goal",
}
```

The card's claim, restated: with this filter armed on top of an unchanged exploration driver, mean collisions per episode drops by at least 50% against `reactive_avoid` on undisclosed-goal exploration scenarios, and holds on drifting-pose scenarios too since only robot-frame lidar is read. Falsified if the reduction is under 50%, or if collisions don't fall at all. The honest cost is `time_to_goal`: at `vx = 0.8` the filter demands 0.40 m of arc clearance beyond the 0.38 m inflation, so tight doorways and cluttered arcs get traversed slower, and the 0.1 m/s grid means a bound command is quantised downward.
